issues.title: kernel_shape missing when exporting to onnx with dynamo=True
issues.author: silverberry-rpi
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

This seems to be the same problem as reported in:
https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/169824
I'm using a onnx to hailo design flow and the missing kernel shape attribute breaks the hailo tools. I verified in netron the attribute kernel_shape is missing when exporting with dynamo=true and when dynamo=false its correctly present and the hailo tools work.
Here's an extra hint, the missing kernel shapes are associated with conv2d layers. When I created these layers I used the size parameter from the yolo.cfg file and passed that int (instead of a h,w tuple) to the layer create. This is interpreted by the conv2d class as a kernel of (size, size). But maybe this causes some confusion in the translator? Just a guess I haven't had time to investigate that yet.
Torch 2.13.0
Onnxscript 0.7.1
Onnx 1.22.0
Here's my call to export that suceeded in outputting the kernel_shape:
torch.onnx.export(model.float(),
                       (model_inputs,),
                       "yolov3.onnx",
                       input_names=["input"],
                       output_names=["output"],
                       export_params=True,
                       training=torch.onnx.TrainingMode.PRESERVE,
                       do_constant_folding=False,
                       opset_version=17,
                       dynamo=False)
The call is full of deprecated arguments because in an effort to solve this problem I  copied it from hailo documentation which seems out of date.

This might require registration to access. Its worth it for the concentrated information.

```python
   def __init__(self):
```

issues.title: [inductor] Wrong Hessian: `torch.compile(torch.func.hessian(f))` miscompiles the derivative of `torch.trace` — a constant is added to every Hessian entry
issues.author: shadow-orange41
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Compiling `torch.func.hessian` with the **inductor** backend produces a wrong Hessian whenever the function contains `torch.trace`. The compiled result equals the correct Hessian plus a constant across (nearly) all entries:

```
H_inductor = H_eager + c * ones(n*n, n*n)
```

The primal value and first-order derivatives (`jacfwd`, `jacrev`) are correct. Only second order is affected. 

### Minimal repro

```python
import torch
from torch.func import hessian

torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)

n = 3

def f(t):
    return torch.mean(1.0 / (t + torch.trace(t) * torch.eye(n, dtype=t.dtype)))

x = torch.tensor([[0.10, 0.20, 0.30],
                  [0.40, 0.50, 0.60],
                  [0.70, 0.80, 0.95]])

H_eager = hessian(f)(x).reshape(n * n, n * n)

H_ind = torch.compile(hessian(f))(x).reshape(n * n, n * n)
print("\neager    row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in H_eager[5].tolist()])
print("inductor row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in H_ind[5].tolist()])
print("diff     row 5:", [f"{v:+.6f}" for v in (H_ind - H_eager)[5].tolist()])
```

### Output

```
eager    row 5: ['+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+1.028807', '+0.000000', '+0.000000', '+0.000000']
inductor row 5: ['+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+1.132515', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708']
diff     row 5: ['+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708', '+0.103708']
```
Note the difference is a CONSTANT smeared across entries: the trace-derivative contribution (identity matrix, diagonal-only) is collapsed to a single scalar and broadcast-added without the eye mask.

```python
                  [0.70, 0.80, 0.95]], dtype=torch.float64)
```

`hessian(f2)` eager: nonzero entries only on (diag, diag) pairs, all 2.0, which is the correct `2 * vec(I) ⊗ vec(I)`. `torch.compile(hessian(f2))`: every entry is 2.0, as if the jacobian basis of `trace` were expanded everywhere.

What is separated out:

- `torch.compile(jacfwd(f2))` and `torch.compile(jacrev(f2))` both match eager exactly (maxdiff 0.0). Only the second-order composition is wrong.
- The `make_fx(jacfwd(f2))` graph builds the basis correctly: `new_zeros(9,9)` + fill main diagonal + `view(9,3,3)` + per-tangent `diagonal(...,1,2)` + `sum([1])`.
- The wrongness enters in inductor's execution of that basis chain: the compiled artifact spreads the per-tangent trace vector as all-ones (so every tangent pair ends up equal), while the dynamo graph for it is correct. The fused cpp kernel (`cpp_fused_arange_diagonal_expand_fill_index_put_mul_new_zeros_pow_sum_trace_view_zeros_0`) is where the fill/expand indexing of the basis gets rewritten.

So the jvp of `trace` is fine; the joint second-order lowering of the basis-building chain (`new_zeros` -> `diagonal` -> `fill_` -> `view` -> `diagonal` -> `sum`) mis-indexes it. Happy to dig at the exact IR mutation if nobody is already on it.

Fixed by PR #191123: the trace decomposition now uses `(self * eye(n)).sum()` instead of `sum(diag(self))`, avoiding the `diagonal_scatter` lowering path that broke under higher-order AD with `torch.compile`.

**Root cause**: `diag.backward()` uses `diagonal_scatter`, which Inductor lowers to `index_put`. Under forward-over-reverse Hessian (`jacfwd(jacrev)`), the JVP of this lowering loses the diagonal structure — the mask collapses to a scalar and broadcasts incorrectly.

**Fix**: Replace the problematic `diag` + `diagonal_scatter` path with an element-wise multiply by `eye(n)`, which Inductor handles correctly at all AD orders.

issues.title: [RFC] DeviceInterface: Registry Support for PrivateUse1 Backends in torch.compile
issues.body:
## TL;DR

This RFC document aims to propose and discuss making PrivateUse1 (out-of-tree) backends first-class citizens in `torch.compile`. Our focus is on eliminating the hardcoded `cuda`/`xpu`/`mps` device lists and if-branches that permeate the Dynamo and Inductor codebase, replacing them with a unified registry-based contract that the eager path already respects. This initiative is split into three independent, reviewable sub-RFCs along the `torch.compile` pipeline — device identity/capability, Dynamo tracing, and Inductor codegen — each addressing a distinct slice of the problem. By aligning with the existing `DeviceInterface` / `DeviceOpOverrides` / entry-point mechanisms, we aim to enable any PrivateUse1 backend that registers via `register_interface_for_device_PrivateUse1` to be automatically recognized by the entire `torch.compile` stack, with zero monkeypatching of upstream module-level lists or dicts.

## Motivation

PyTorch's eager path already has a device extension contract for PrivateUse1 backends: register a device module, dispatch ops, expose runtime APIs + `DeviceInterface`, and the backend becomes a first-class device. This has enabled out-of-tree backends like `torch_npu`, `torch_mlu`, and others to integrate with PyTorch's eager mode. However, `torch.compile` (Dynamo + Inductor) **ignores this contract** and instead checks hardcoded `cuda`/`xpu`/`mps` device lists and if-branches at every layer.

This creates a **structural contradiction**: a backend already recognized in eager mode (e.g., a hypothetical accelerator `acc`) is invisible at compile time — treated as "not GPU", "can't run Triton", "untraceable", "device nyi". The only workaround today is monkeypatching upstream module-level lists/dicts/private functions, which is fragile, untested by upstream CI, drifts on every refactor, and contradicts the first-class citizen goal. As more PrivateUse1 backends emerge, this problem scales worse — each backend independently patches the same upstream symbols, creating maintenance burden and breakage risk.

Therefore, we upstream the registry-based device contract into `torch.compile` itself, so that any PrivateUse1 backend that registers via `register_interface_for_device_PrivateUse1` is automatically recognized by the entire compile stack. This will facilitate the out-of-box experience for PrivateUse1 backend users and benefit the PyTorch community by making `torch.compile` truly device-agnostic.

## Approach

Eventually, we will fully support PrivateUse1 backends in `torch.compile` for both inference and training, in both `torch.compile` mode and eager mode. From an execution perspective, we split the problem into three independent slices along the `torch.compile` pipeline, each landable and reviewable on its own:

1. **Device identity/capability** (RFC 1): Before dispatching to any backend, Inductor must determine the device's identity (is it a GPU?) and capabilities (can it run Triton? how many compute units? does it need guards?). Today these checks query hardcoded lists; we change them to query `get_interface_for_device(device).is_gpu()` and similar contract methods.

2. **Dynamo tracing** (RFC 2): When Dynamo symbolically executes Python into an FX graph, it must recognize device-related types (tensor classes, `Stream`, `Event`) and runtime functions (`current_stream`, `synchronize`, `get_device_properties`). Today six lookup tables hardcode CUDA/XPU; we splice them from the registry.

3. **Inductor codegen** (RFC 3): When Inductor codegens an optimized FX graph into device-specific compilable code, it must discover the backend, accept per-device configuration, compile C++ wrappers with the right include/lib/definitions, and contribute device info to cache keys and autotune env. Today all of these hardcode CUDA; we provide registration interfaces via `DeviceOpOverrides` and `DeviceInterface` extensions.

In addition, we have added a shared registration primitive — `register_interface_for_device_PrivateUse1` + `get_interface_for_device` — to `torch/_dynamo/device_interface.py` that all three sub-RFCs build upon. Built-in devices (`cuda`, `xpu`, `cpu`, `mps`, `mtia`, `meta`) are locked down by `_BUILTIN_DEVICE_INIT_LIST`; out-of-tree extensions must target a PrivateUse1 device type.

In summary, the scope of this umbrella RFC is as follows:

- Three sub-RFCs, each independently reviewable and landable
- Shared registration primitive: `register_interface_for_device_PrivateUse1` + `get_interface_for_device`
- New capability bits on `DeviceInterface`: `is_gpu()`, `exposes_streams()`, `get_multi_processor_count()`, `visible_devices_env()`, `get_cache_system_info()`, `dynamo_tensor_classes`, `dynamo_constant_fold_fns[_need_guards]`
- Extensions to `DeviceOpOverrides`: `get_cpp_torch_device_options`, `aten_device_type`, `cpp_stream_type`
- New entry-point group `torch_inductor_backends` for backend auto-discovery
- All new methods have safe defaults (`False`, `None`, empty tuple/list) — a backend that registers with minimal slots doesn't break anything
- in-tree backends declare capability bits, precisely reproducing current behavior (zero behavior change)
- **Out of scope**: AOTInductor C-shim ABI (`aoti_torch_<device>_<op>`) — needs a separate proposal

## Components

Since we are taking a pipeline-sliced approach, we have identified three crucial components, each corresponding to one sub-RFC:

- **Device Identity/Capability Contract** – This component is the cornerstone to support all downstream compile-stack decisions. It provides the registration entry (`register_interface_for_device_PrivateUse1`), the extended query function (`get_interface_for_device`), and capability bits on `DeviceInterface` (`is_gpu`, `is_triton_capable`, `exposes_streams`, `get_multi_processor_count`). Without this, no other component can make device-aware decisions.

- **Dynamo Registry Splicing** – Although Dynamo has some registry-aware code paths (e.g., `builder.py` already iterates `get_registered_device_interfaces()`), six critical lookup tables still hardcode CUDA/XPU. This component splices all six tables from the registry, introduces `get_interface_for_device__PrivateUse1()` for iterating only PrivateUse1 devices, and adds the `register_device_trace_rules()` public entry for backend runtime function trace rules.

- **Inductor Codegen Registration Interfaces** – Inductor's codegen path has no end-to-end backend discovery, rejects third-party config keys, and hardcodes branches in cpp-builder/AOTI/wrapper/autotune/cache-key. This component provides four registration interfaces: entry-point discovery, per-device config routing, `DeviceOpOverrides` contract extensions, and `DeviceInterface` runtime methods.

Besides the three components above, we rely on the existing `DeviceInterface` and `DeviceOpOverrides` contracts that PyTorch already defines for eager mode. No parallel mechanism is created.

## Design

In this section, we present a high-level design for each component. Regarding the detailed design, please refer to the dedicated sub-RFC for each component for more information.

### Device Identity/Capability Contract

PyTorch's `torch.compile` stack determines device identity and capabilities through hardcoded lists: `GPU_TYPES = ["cuda", "mps", "xpu", "mtia"]` for `is_gpu`, a `triton_supported_devices` dict for `has_triton`, and `if device_type == "xpu"/"mtia"` fallbacks for `multi_processor_count`. In terms of PrivateUse1 backends, we will replace all these with `get_interface_for_device(device).is_gpu()` and similar contract method calls. We add an `is_gpu()` capability bit to `DeviceInterface` (default `False`, parallel to the existing `is_triton_capable()`). The `GPU_TYPES` list is retained as a late-binding compatibility shim backed by a private `_gpu_types()` that iterates the registry — no new public function is added. The `assert len(avail_gpus) <= 1` in `get_gpu_type()` is replaced by a disambiguation rule (reuse `torch.accelerator.current_accelerator()` priority, PrivateUse1 first). The `!= "mps"` literal in `device_need_guard` is replaced by `_exposes_streams(device)`, which checks whether `iface.Stream is not DeviceInterface.Stream`.

Please refer to the dedicated RFC #189135 for detailed design elaboration.

### Dynamo Registry Splicing

Dynamo answers two questions for every value/call during symbolic execution: "what is it" (which `VariableTracker` wraps it) and "how to handle it" (inline / emit FX node / constant-fold / graph-break). Six lookup tables answer these questions, and all hardcode CUDA/XPU. We will splice all six from the registry: `_in_graph_classes` splices `dynamo_tensor_classes` / `Stream` / `Event` from all registered interfaces; stream variable class uses generic `StreamVariable` + `native_handle` default path (out-of-tree: zero subclass, zero slot), with the `native_handle` fallback lifted from inside the `"cuda_stream"` branch to the generic base; `trace_rules` gets a new `register_device_trace_rules()` public entry; constant-fold groups use two optional tuple slots on `DeviceInterface`; `common_constant_types` derives properties class from `type(iface.get_device_properties(...))`. The only non-derivable information — dtype-specialized tensor types — is handled by one optional slot `dynamo_tensor_classes` (default empty, safe).

Please refer to the dedicated RFC #189136 for detailed design elaboration.

### Inductor Codegen Registration Interfaces

Inductor's codegen path has four things that lack registration interfaces. We will address all four: (1) backend discovery via new entry-point group `torch_inductor_backends`, loaded in `init_backend_registration()` (failure is warning-only); (2) per-device config `apply_options` accepting registered keys by prefix (e.g., `"acc_backend.flag"`); (3) C++ compile options and AOTI device mapping via `DeviceOpOverrides` contract extensions (`get_cpp_torch_device_options`, `aten_device_type` default `at::kPrivateUse1`, `cpp_stream_type`); (4) runtime/host misc via `DeviceInterface` methods (`visible_devices_env` default `None`, `get_cache_system_info` default `None`). The four autotune sites that hardcode `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` are unified through `visible_devices_env()`. The two-pass compilation gate in `graph.py` uses `is_gpu(device)` (depends on RFC 1). We follow existing `DeviceOpOverrides` / `DeviceInterface` / entry-point mechanisms — no parallel mechanism is created.

**Honest boundary**: AOTInductor has an additional C-shim ABI layer (`aoti_torch_<device>_<op>`) that this RFC **cannot** address. `get_c_shim_func_name` directly concatenates `aoti_torch_{device}_{op}` without going through `DEVICE_TO_ATEN` fallback. No-c-shim backends will still fail AOTI at link time. This needs a separate proposal.

Please refer to the dedicated RFC #189137 for detailed design elaboration.

For a more comprehensive and detailed understanding of each component's design, we highly encourage you to explore the respective sub-RFCs linked above. These documents provide in-depth insight and technical specifics that are crucial for a complete grasp of the proposed implementations and integrations.

comments.author: myfykris
comments.body:
> We already have support for out-of-tree backends, though perhaps there are some gaps relating to PrivateUse1. Smaller patches that remove device hardcodings are welcome. I think this is mostly all that would be needed to fix PrivateUse1 issues.
>
> If you think bigger changes are needed, please provide more details -- especially compared to the existing out-of-tree backend support. I'd much rather extend what is already there than add some sort of parallel registration system.

I completely agree that extending the existing backend interfaces is preferable to introducing a parallel registration mechanism. I don't think another registration system is needed.

Where I think we may be aiming a little too narrowly is in the scope.

To me, this isn't fundamentally a `torch.compile` problem. It's a PyTorch-wide backend capability problem.

`torch.compile` is one consumer of backend capabilities, but so are eager execution, backend dispatch, optimization selection, and libraries built on top of PyTorch. If the capability abstraction only exists inside `torch.compile`, every other consumer will continue solving the same problem independently.

The reason I think this matters is that a surprising number of backend checks are not actually backend checks. They're capability checks expressed as backend checks because there isn't currently a first-class capability interface available.

For example, in Inductor there is:

```python
def prepare_softmax_extra_check(match):
    """
    We only have triton online softmax kernels currently.
    """
    device_type = match.kwargs["x"].meta["val"].device.type
    return (
        config.online_softmax
        and device_type in ["cuda", "xpu"]
        and getattr(config, f"{device_type}_backend") == "triton"
    )
```

The capability being queried here is the availability of an online-softmax implementation.

CUDA is not an online-softmax algorithm.

XPU is not an online-softmax algorithm.

Triton is not an online-softmax algorithm.

Those are simply implementation choices that currently happen to provide an online-softmax implementation. Another backend could provide exactly the same capability through native kernels, another compiler, generated code, or a vendor library. The logical requirement is "an online-softmax implementation is available," but the current mechanism infers that from backend identity and implementation details.

The same pattern already exists outside PyTorch.

Transformers has accumulated a growing collection of backend, package, and feature discovery helpers such as `is_flash_attn_2_available()`, `is_flash_linear_attention_available()`, `is_causal_conv1d_available()`, `is_torch_bf16_available_on_device()`, and many others. Those functions are effectively an ad hoc capability and availability layer implemented outside of PyTorch because downstream libraries have no common capability interface they can query.

Even more interesting is what happens inside model implementations themselves.

Recent Qwen3.5 models determine whether their optimized gated-delta attention path is available by checking whether CUDA-oriented packages like `causal-conv1d` and `flash-linear-attention` can be imported, then binding function pointers from those packages into the model class.

But those models do not fundamentally require those packages.

They require implementations of causal convolution, incremental causal-convolution update, chunked gated-delta attention, and recurrent gated-delta attention.

Those operations could be provided by any backend.

Today, however, there is no PyTorch capability interface that allows a backend to advertise those capabilities or a model to discover them. Under the current design, a non-CUDA backend cannot provide equivalent optimized implementations through the existing backend interface. It has to modify Transformers, inject or replace the stored function pointers, or fall back to the generic implementation. That seems like a strong indication that the abstraction is missing at the framework level rather than simply requiring a few additional backend integrations.

This is why I don't think removing hardcoded backend checks one at a time completely solves the problem. Even if every remaining check inside `torch.compile` were replaced, downstream projects would continue writing backend-name checks, package checks, version checks, runtime probes, and library-specific capability systems because they have no common capability interface to use instead.

I wonder if this RFC could become the foundation of a PyTorch-wide backend capability system, with `torch.compile` being one consumer rather than the owner of that abstraction.

I also think the capability interface itself probably needs to be richer than simple booleans.

Many capabilities are conditional. Support often depends on the exact operation and its inputs.

Conceptually, capability queries are closer to:

```python
supports(
    op=torch.ops.aten.scaled_dot_product_attention,
    device=device,
    dtype=torch.float16,
    layout=torch.strided,
    head_dim=128,
    is_causal=True,
    mask_type="none",
)
```

than:

```python
supports_sdpa = True
```

Similarly, implementation selection should become capability negotiation rather than backend detection. Higher-level code should be able to request an implementation satisfying a set of requirements instead of enumerating backend names.

I'm not proposing a second registration mechanism. I'd like to see the existing backend interfaces become the authoritative source for capability discovery so both PyTorch itself and the broader ecosystem have something better to query than backend identity or package availability.

To me, the remaining backend-specific checks throughout the ecosystem aren't the root problem. They're evidence that backend identity and package availability are currently being used as substitutes for capability because capability isn't yet a first-class concept in PyTorch.

Thanks for the review — let me make sure I'm capturing your intent correctly.

You're proposing that `BackendFeature` be promoted to a torch-wide public capability-check abstraction, and that the various hand-maintained device-name lists be replaced by queries against it. For example, the `_get_capturable_supported_devices` you referenced could become:

```python
def _get_capturable_supported_devices(supports_xla: bool = True) -> list[str]:
    return [d for d, _ in get_registered_device_interfaces()
            if ":" not in d
            and has_backend_feature(d, BackendFeature.CAPTURABLE_OPTIMIZER)] \
           + (["xla"] if supports_xla and not torch.jit.is_scripting() else [])
```

And the `GPU_TYPES` list I referenced earlier would likewise be derived from the registry instead of hardcoded, by extending the promoted `BackendFeature` enum with a `GPU` member:

```python
class BackendFeature(Enum):
    # —— original Inductor codegen capabilities (migrated from common.py) ——
    FOREACH = auto()
    BUCKETIZE = auto()
    INPLACE_BUFFERS = auto()
    MASKED_SCATTER_WITH_INDEX = auto()
    SCAN = auto()
    SORT = auto()
    TUPLE_REDUCTION = auto()
    PREFER_STORE_LOOP_ORDER = auto()
    TRITON_TEMPLATES = auto()
    REDUCE_TO_SINGLE_ELEMENT = auto()
    # —— framework-level (incl. eager) capabilities ——
    GPU = auto()

GPU_TYPES=[name for name, iface in get_registered_device_interfaces()
 if ":" not in name                          # only device-type names, skip "cuda:0"
 and BackendFeature.GPU in iface.backend_features(None)]
```

So before I revise the RFC, I'd like to confirm with you: is the thrust of your proposal to consolidate the **boolean** capability queries across the framework into this single promoted `BackendFeature` abstraction, with `DeviceInterface` remaining the reporter for the eager path (since `get_backend_features()` today delegates to the Inductor `Scheduling` class, which isn't instantiated on the eager path)?

One honest boundary I want to flag: non-boolean capabilities (e.g. `get_multi_processor_count()` → int, `visible_devices_env()` → str, `dynamo_tensor_classes` → types) can't be expressed as enum membership, so those would still live as `DeviceInterface` methods. Does that match your thinking, or would you scope it differently?

comments.author: myfykris
comments.body:
> You're proposing that `BackendFeature` be promoted to a torch-wide public capability-check abstraction

Yes.

I'll be honest, my motivation for this comes directly from building a fairly complete PrivateUse1 backend for Apple/Metal since November. It's reached the point where capability discovery has become a bigger obstacle than implementing kernels and a workload-aware dispatch layer that selects optimized implementations for operations like `matmul`, `eigh`, `svd`, `sort`, etc.

The good news is that I haven't been blocked. I've been able to work around these cases by monkeypatching PyTorch, Transformers, and model-specific classes. The bad news is that I have to monkeypatch them in the first place.

A recurring pattern has been that an optimized path is gated on CUDA when the real requirement is simply that the backend supports a particular optimized implementation. Without a canonical capability interface, the only way for any backend, whether in-tree or out-of-tree, to expose those capabilities today is to patch the framework or the libraries consuming it.

I don't believe booleans are the end state, though. I think the capability interface will eventually need to be **richer**, as I mentioned above. That said, starting with boolean capabilities may be the pragmatic choice. It would allow the abstraction to be introduced and adopted incrementally without requiring every conditional or parameterized capability question to be solved up front.

One concrete example is Flash Linear Attention in Transformers/Qwen. My backend has a complete Flash Linear Attention implementation, but it cannot be selected through the supported Transformers/Qwen path unless I monkeypatch either Transformers or the Qwen model class, because `transformers/utils/import_utils.py` currently contains:

```python
def is_flash_linear_attention_available():
    is_available, fla_version = _is_package_available("fla", return_version=True)
    return (
        is_torch_cuda_available()
        and is_available
        and version.parse(fla_version) >= version.parse("0.2.2")
    )
```

The capability the model actually needs is: *"Does the active backend provide Flash Linear Attention?"* Instead, the decision is made by asking whether CUDA is available and whether a CUDA-oriented package is installed. Since there is no supported mechanism for a backend to advertise that capability, the optimized implementation cannot be discovered and used without monkeypatching.

One thing I like about promoting something like **`BackendFeature`** is that it doesn't have to become mandatory immediately. Libraries could first ask the capability interface and, if the capability isn't defined yet, simply fall back to today's existing checks. That lets the capability vocabulary evolve over time without breaking existing code, while giving backends a standard way to advertise what they support.

That's really the problem I'm trying to solve. My examples happen to come from a PrivateUse1 backend because that's what I've been building, but I think the underlying architectural problem is broader than PrivateUse1 itself.

EDIT: I realized I didn't quite answer your question as asked about only doing boolean values and having the non-boolean stuff sequestered in the DeviceInterface methods.  No, I'm not suggesting that we have two places where one is boolean and the other is able to handle complex values.  I'm just suggesting boolean first, to get at least yes/no capability advertising functionality first.  Then add the richer expression capabilities later.  I would be overjoyed if v1 of this included those extended capability mapping functionalities from the start.

comments.author: jansel
comments.body:
BackendFeature itself might not be right here, because it is defined per inductor backend.  While here you are really querying properties of whatever eager PrivateUse1 backend is registered.  So ideally you could change through dispatcher registration without needing to register something in inductor.

Perhaps the most similar thing is [torch.accelerator.get_device_capability](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/2.13/generated/torch.accelerator.get_device_capability.html#torch.accelerator.get_device_capability).  See #143887 for more discussion on that.

I could imagine a lot of the examples above being migrated to `get_device_capability`-based checks.  I'm hesitant to add something new here just because of how much similar stuff has been done in the past.

cc @albanD @ezyang as this seems more like an eager-mode request than a compile one

comments.author: myfykris
comments.body:
After looking into `torch.accelerator.get_device_capability()` I have to agree that it's probably a better starting point for this than `BackendFeature`.  It's already public and device specific and even PrivateUse1 backends can integrate.

That being said, even though the docs say `dict[str, Any]` return type, the registered backend need to return the fixed `c10::DeviceCapability` structure, and that only has dtype capability bits atm.

So, yeah, I think you're right and this is likely the better place to start, thanks!.  Just need to extend it some before an out-of-tree backend could advertise capabilities such as FLA or online softmax.

One thing to note, and maybe I'm reading too much into your "eager" qualifier, but I'm running into issues around this for both eager and compiled modes.  In the Qwen example, the implementation selection branch happens in Transformers/model code before either path reaches the backend, so I have to monkeypatch it for both.

EDIT: While looking into this further I realized the Qwen example actually highlights two issues, not just one. For Qwen, capability discovery alone doesn't solve it because there's also no backend-neutral PyTorch API for Gated DeltaNet attention like there is for `scaled_dot_product_attention` that backends can implement through the dispatcher. I think this particular example shows the need for both a capability interface AND one or more new canonical operators. Capability discovery is still independently an issue for operators that PyTorch already has though.

Thanks for the pointer to `torch.accelerator.get_device_capability()` — I did look into it carefully before settling on the `BackendFeature` route, but I'd like to push back gently and explain why I think `BackendFeature` is the right choice for this RFC.

## 1. `BackendFeature` already *is* the inductor-backend capability interface

The enum lives in `torch/_inductor/codegen/common.py` and is consumed throughout inductor (`has_backend_feature`, `V.graph.has_feature`, `get_backend_features(device)`, etc.). It is the established channel for "does this inductor codegen backend support FOREACH / BUCKETIZE / SCAN / SORT / TRITON_TEMPLATES / ...". The hardcoded lists this RFC is trying to eliminate (e.g. `GPU_TYPES` in `torch/_inductor/utils.py:100`) all live on the inductor side as well. So extending `BackendFeature` keeps the fix within the same layer it is trying to un-hardcode, which is exactly the scope of this RFC. It does not try to redefine torch-wide capability discovery.

## 2. `torch.accelerator.get_device_capability()` is the right *idea*, but is not reliably usable today

Conceptually it is a cleaner, cross-torch public entry point, and I agree it is the better long-term home. In practice it currently errors out on backends you would expect to work — including plain CUDA:

```
>>> capabilities = torch.accelerator.get_device_capability("cuda:0")
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File ".../torch/accelerator/__init__.py", line 185, in get_device_capability
    return torch._C._accelerator_getDeviceCapability(device_index)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
RuntimeError: Backend doesn't support getting device capabilities.
```

The root cause is that several `GuardImpl`s (notably CUDA's `CUDAGuardImpl`) do not override `getDeviceCapability`, so dispatch falls through to the base-class stub in `c10/core/impl/DeviceGuardImplInterface.h:211`, which unconditionally raises `TORCH_CHECK(false, "Backend doesn't support getting device capabilities.")`. The underlying `c10::DeviceCapability` struct (`c10/core/DeviceCapability.h:46`) also only carries dtype bits today, so it cannot yet express "is a GPU-class device" without a separate extension pass over the C++ struct, every backend's `GuardImpl`, and the pybind binding in `torch/csrc/DeviceAccelerator.cpp`.

Layering this RFC on top of `get_device_capability()` would therefore couple a self-contained inductor de-hardcoding fix to a broader, still-unstable stabilization effort spanning c10 / ATen / torch accelerators. That is a larger surface than this RFC intends to touch.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

This appears to be related to #173902, but the issue is still reproducible on newer PyTorch versions.

I attached a simplified repro archive.

The repro compares a CUDA fp32 eager Conv2d result with a CUDA fp16 compiled Conv2d result using Inductor shape padding. The output shows a large numerical divergence.

I verified this on both PyTorch 2.10.0+cu126 and PyTorch 2.12.1+cu126.

Only the PyTorch version/environment was changed; the repro itself was otherwise unchanged.

Actual behavior:

```text
Conv1 RelDiff > 1e-4: True (1.6850e+00)
```

Expected behavior:

The compiled CUDA fp16 Conv2d result should not diverge this much from the CUDA fp32 eager reference.

Versions tested:

- PyTorch 2.10.0+cu126
- PyTorch 2.12.1+cu126

Related issue:

- #173902
‘’‘python
import os
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
def max_relative_error(a, b):
    a = a.detach().cpu().float()
    b = b.detach().cpu().float()
    diff = torch.abs(a - b)
    rel_diff = diff / torch.clamp(torch.abs(a), min=1e-12)
    return rel_diff.max().item()
def make_conv(dtype):
    layer = nn.Conv2d(3, 96, 3, stride=2, padding=1).cuda().to(dtype)
    sd = torch.load("sd.pt", map_location="cpu")

    x_fp32 = x.cuda().float()

        out_fp32 = eager_fp32(x_fp32)
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_SHAPE_PADDING"] = "1"
        compiled_fp16 = torch.compile(make_conv(torch.float16))
        out_fp16 = compiled_fp16(x_fp16)
    max_rd = max_relative_error(out_fp32, out_fp16)
    print(f"Conv1 RelDiff > 1e-4: {max_rd > 1e-4} ({max_rd:.4e})")

issues.author: zifan6699
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

I found a numerical stability issue where `nn.LSTM` produces NaNs when running on CUDA (Eager mode), but works correctly on CPU (Compiled with Inductor) using the same input and weights. The input tensor is verified to be valid (no NaNs or Infs), and the relative L2 difference between inputs across devices is zero.

- Mode A (Eager CUDA): Produces NaN output.
- Mode B (Compiled CPU): Produces valid numerical output.

This divergence suggests a potential stability issue or bug in the CUDA kernel implementation for LSTM under specific input conditions.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import os
import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def set_inductor_env_vars(env_str: str):
    original_env = os.environ.copy()
    try:
        s = (env_str or "0000")[:4].ljust(4, "0")
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_FALLBACK_RANDOM"] = "1" if s[0] == "1" else "0"
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_EPILOGUE_FUSION"] = "1" if s[1] == "1" else "0"
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_SHAPE_PADDING"] = "1" if s[2] == "1" else "0"
        os.environ["INDUCTOR_DYNAMIC"] = "1" if s[3] == "1" else "0"
        yield
    finally:
        os.environ.clear()
        os.environ.update(original_env)

def get_rel_l2(a, b):
    a = a.detach().cpu().float()
    b = b.detach().cpu().float()
    diff_norm = torch.norm(a - b)
    base_norm = torch.norm(a) + 1e-12
    return (diff_norm / base_norm).item()

def reproduce_lstm_nan_comparison():
    bundle_path = "bundle.pt"
    weight_path = "lstm1_weights.pt"
    bundle = torch.load(bundle_path, map_location="cpu")
    mini_sd = torch.load(weight_path, map_location="cpu")
    x_input = bundle["input_cpu_fp32"]

    print("\n>>> Running Mode A (cuda/float32/0000) ...")
    lstm_a = nn.LSTM(input_size=50, hidden_size=50, num_layers=1, batch_first=True, bidirectional=False).to("cuda").to(torch.float32)
    lstm_a.load_state_dict(mini_sd)
    lstm_a.eval()
    
    with torch.no_grad():
        x_a = x_input.to("cuda").to(torch.float32)
        has_nan_input_a = torch.isnan(x_a).any().item()
        output_a, _ = lstm_a(x_a)
        has_nan_a = torch.isnan(output_a).any().item()
        print(f"Mode A input has NaN: {has_nan_input_a}, output has NaN: {has_nan_a}")

    print("\n>>> Running Mode B (cpu/float32/1000) ...")
    lstm_b = nn.LSTM(input_size=50, hidden_size=50, num_layers=1, batch_first=True, bidirectional=False).to("cpu").to(torch.float32)
    lstm_b.load_state_dict(mini_sd)
    lstm_b.eval()
    
    with set_inductor_env_vars("1000"):
        run_b = torch.compile(lstm_b)
        with torch.no_grad():
            x_b = x_input.to("cpu").to(torch.float32)
            has_nan_input_b = torch.isnan(x_b).any().item()
            output_b, _ = run_b(x_b)
            has_nan_b = torch.isnan(output_b).any().item()
            print(f"Mode B input has NaN: {has_nan_input_b}, output has NaN: {has_nan_b}")

    print("\n" + "="*50)
    print(f"Input Relative Difference (Rel L2): {get_rel_l2(x_a, x_b):.4e}")
    print("="*50)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    reproduce_lstm_nan_comparison()
```

issues.author: zifan6699
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Summary:
When using torch.compile with cpu device and float16 precision, LayerNorm produces NaN outputs when the input contains Inf values. This behavior is inconsistent with the CUDA backend and Eager mode, where numerical stability is better maintained.
Observation:
In our reproduction, Mode A (CUDA float32) works correctly. In Mode B (CPU float16 with Inductor optimization), the input already contains Inf due to float16 overflow. However, instead of maintaining Inf or handling it gracefully, the compiled LayerNorm transforms these Inf values into NaN.
Comparison:
Mode A (CUDA/f32): Input OK -> Output OK
Mode B (CPU/f16): Input has Inf -> Output has NaN (Numerical collapse)

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import os
import contextlib

@contextlib.contextmanager
def set_env(env_str: str):
    original = os.environ.copy()
    s = (env_str or "0000")[:4].ljust(4, "0")
    os.environ.update({
        "INDUCTOR_FALLBACK_RANDOM": "1" if s[0] == "1" else "0",
        "INDUCTOR_EPILOGUE_FUSION": "1" if s[1] == "1" else "0",
```

  - Eager mode remains numerically stable and produces finite outputs.
  - torch.compile (Inductor) produces NaNs for the same inputs, even in FP32.
  
This strongly suggests that the fused Inductor kernel is:
  - Reordering reductions (mean / variance)
  - Potentially computing E[x²] - (E[x])² directly
  - Hitting INF - INF → NaN due to reduced numerical headroom

What makes this particularly confusing for users is that:
  - creds.scopes-style signals aside (i.e. everything appears correct),
  - Eager and compiled modes silently diverge without warning,
  - And the failure only appears at extreme but valid FP32 values.

Even if this behavior is considered acceptable or hard to fix in the compiler, it would be extremely helpful to explicitly document this limitation like:
  - That Inductor-fused LayerNorm may be numerically unstable for inputs close to FP32 limits
  - That eager mode uses more conservative kernels / accumulation order
  - Or that users should rescale / clamp inputs or disable compile for LN in such cases

From a user perspective, the lack of documentation makes this hard to diagnose — especially since the same model behaves correctly in eager mode.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Description

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import os

def run():
    x, sd = torch.load("input.pt"), torch.load("sd.pt")
    layer = nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, stride=2, padding=1, bias=False)

The new reproduction script runs across CPU Eager, CPU Compile, CUDA Eager, CUDA Compile (eager, aot_eager and inductor) backends, then prints a pairwise relative error matrix. It shows two clusters: {CPU Eager, CPU Compile, CUDA inductor} agree bit-exactly, while {CUDA Eager, CUDA Compile_eager, CUDA aot_eager} agree among themselves but diverge from the first group.

To determine the root cause the below script is helpful
```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F


def rel_err(a, b):
    return ((a - b).abs() / torch.max(a.abs(), b.abs()).clamp(min=1e-12)).max().item()


def make_conv(scale):
    torch.manual_seed(42)
    x = torch.randn(1, 3, 224, 224) * scale
    w = torch.randn(32, 3, 3, 3)
    return x, w


def run():
    x, w = make_conv(2.5e11)

    with torch.no_grad():
        cpu = F.conv2d(x, w, stride=2, padding=1).float()

        cuda_nchw = F.conv2d(x.cuda(), w.cuda(), stride=2, padding=1).cpu().float()
        cuda_nhwc = F.conv2d(
            x.cuda().to(memory_format=torch.channels_last),
            w.cuda().to(memory_format=torch.channels_last),
            stride=2, padding=1,
        ).cpu().float()

    print("NCHW vs CPU:", rel_err(cuda_nchw, cpu))
    print("NHWC vs CPU:", rel_err(cuda_nhwc, cpu))
    print("NHWC bit-exact:", torch.equal(cuda_nhwc, cpu))

    # TF32 check
    with torch.no_grad():
        orig = (
            torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32,
            torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32,
        )
        torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
        torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = False
        cuda_no_tf32 = F.conv2d(x.cuda(), w.cuda(), stride=2, padding=1).cpu().float()
        torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32, torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = orig

    print("TF32 irrelevant:", torch.equal(cuda_no_tf32, cuda_nchw))

    # cuDNN vs native CUDA
    with torch.no_grad(), torch.backends.cudnn.flags(enabled=False):
        cuda_native = F.conv2d(x.cuda(), w.cuda(), stride=2, padding=1).cpu().float()

    print("cuDNN irrelevant:", torch.equal(cuda_native, cuda_nchw))

    # CPU layout invariance
    with torch.no_grad():
        cpu_nhwc = F.conv2d(
            x.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last),
            w.to(memory_format=torch.channels_last),
            stride=2, padding=1,
        ).float()

    print("CPU layout invariant:", torch.equal(cpu, cpu_nhwc))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run()
```

Output:
```
NCHW vs CPU: 0.7746869921684265
NHWC vs CPU: 0.0
NHWC bit-exact: True
TF32 irrelevant: True
cuDNN irrelevant: True
CPU layout invariant: True
```
The above script isolates the root cause by stripping away backends and testing F.conv2d directly with controlled memory layouts. It proves:
- Passing the same tensors as NHWC (channels-last) to CUDA matches CPU bit-exactly; NCHW does not
- Disabling TF32 changes nothing
- Disabling cuDNN (Slow2d fallback = im2col + cuBLAS) gives the same divergent result as cuDNN NCHW
- CPU is layout-insensitive (NCHW == NHWC bit-exactly)

**Conclusion:**
Inductor converts tensors to NHWC before calling cuDNN. Eager passes them as NCHW. cuDNN picks a different engine for each layout, and those engines give different floating-point results. 
Hence the gap is not a bug in PyTorch's eager or inductor paths, both call the same cudnn_convolution through the same aten::convolution dispatch. The difference is that cuDNN itself selects different internal algorithms depending on the memory layout it receives, and those algorithms add up the same numbers in a different order. Since floating-point addition is not associative, different orders produce slightly different results.

**Solution**
In my opinion this is expected floating-point behavior and not a correctness bug. Rather than changing the default layout or forcing to adhere to same layout even when not required may not be the right thing to do. This should be documented properly and user should be made aware via a warning or throwing an error about the divergence and that it is expected to be like this. User may enfore the memory layout if they need strictly matching execution patterns. 

P.S. - I am open to any better suggestions and would gladly implement if any better solution is there for this problem.

issues.title: [`SDPA`] Checking for FA backend eligibility via SDPAParams fails under fullgraph compile
issues.author: vasqu
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Currently, the `enable_gqa` using torch sdpa is only viable for the FA and math backend (also probably cuDNN but doesn't really matter here) so we actually only want to use this feature when we know that FA will be invoked as the math backend is too slow compared to the mem-efficient path (with manually repeated kv groups).

We had naive assumptions first, e.g. no mask + viable version. But this is not sufficient, because there are other possible breaking conditions e.g. different seq_lens or head dims. The idea was then to use the native torch checking functions see https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/pull/45776 (because manually keeping track of these will be unmaintainable imo)

However, based on our CI (https://app.circleci.com/pipelines/github/huggingface/transformers/174021/workflows/0632f33d-6844-4576-a08c-04ccbda483de/jobs/2300522 Edit: was on run on CPU so ran into a wrong conditional local cuda GPU failure remains) you can see that a fullgraph test is failing, i.e. `tests/models/glm_ocr/test_modeling_glm_ocr.py::GlmOcrModelTest::test_generate_compile_model_forward_fullgraph`. It seems (to me) that this is related to the `SDPAParams` object not being fully traceable - which honestly shouldn't be the case, no? 

The reproducer hence is to run the aforementioned test on that branch of transformers. I have also verified this locally e.g.
```py
import os

import pytest

os.environ["RUN_SLOW"] = "1"

model = "glm_ocr"
pytest.main([f"tests/models/{model}/test_modeling_{model}.py", "-k", "test_generate_compile_model_forward_fullgraph"])
```
